title: Redox Reactions
seo_title: Grade 11 Physical Sciences: Redox Reactions Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_text: Oxidation as a loss of electrons and reduction as a gain of electrons; oxidation numbers; oxidising and reducing agents; writing and balancing redox half-reactions and overall equations; the table of standard reduction potentials to predict reactions. (summary of CAPS Physical Sciences, Grade 11, Chemistry: Redox reactions)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Physical Sciences worksheets (CAPS): oxidation and reduction, oxidation numbers, oxidising and reducing agents and half-reactions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons.
body_html:
How to think about it

Oxidation is a loss of electrons (the oxidation number increases); reduction is a gain of electrons (the oxidation number decreases). Oxidation and reduction always happen together. Oxidation numbers: elements are 0, O is usually −2, H is usually +1, and they add up to the charge of the species.

The oxidising agent takes electrons and is itself reduced; the reducing agent gives electrons and is itself oxidised. Half-reactions show the electrons; the electrons lost must equal the electrons gained in the overall equation.

Example

Oxidation number of Mn in MnO₄⁻?

x + 4(−2) = −1

Answer: +7

Example

Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Which is oxidised?

Which loses electrons?

Answer: zinc

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the oxidising agent is oxidised.
  • Forgetting that oxidation numbers add up to the charge.
  • Not balancing the electrons in half-reactions.

faq.q: Why is chlorine used to treat water?
faq.a: It is a strong oxidising agent that kills bacteria.

items.q: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, which is the oxidising agent?
items.e: O₂ gains electrons (is reduced), so it is the oxidising agent; Mg is the reducing agent.

items.q: In Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂, which is the oxidising agent?
items.e: Cl₂ gains electrons (is reduced), so it is the oxidising agent; KI (I⁻) is the reducing agent.

items.q: In 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, which is the reducing agent?
items.e: Al loses electrons (is oxidised), so it is the reducing agent.

items.q: In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, which is the reducing agent?
items.e: CO loses electrons (is oxidised), so it is the reducing agent.

items.q: What is reduction?
c: gain of electrons (or a decrease in oxidation number)
items.e: The oxidising agent is reduced.

items.q: What is the oxidation state of I in IO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>?
items.e: Oxygen is −2 (−1 in peroxides), hydrogen +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); the total equals the charge on the species.

items.q: What is the oxidation number of an element in its uncombined state?
items.e: For example, O₂ and Fe have 0.

items.q: What happens when a strip of zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution?
c: copper forms on the zinc and the blue colour fades
the solution turns green and hydrogen forms
items.e: Zinc is more reactive than copper.

items.q: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, which is the reducing agent?
items.e: H₂ loses electrons (is oxidised), so it is the reducing agent.

items.q: Why is rusting a redox reaction?

items.e: Water and oxygen are both needed.

items.q: A piece of iron is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Will a displacement reaction occur? (Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au)
c: No. Iron is less active than copper, so no reaction occurs.
Yes. Any metal replaces any other metal.
Yes. Iron is more active than copper, so it replaces it.
No. Metals never react with solutions.
items.e: A metal replaces only metals below it in the reactivity series.
